::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Theme: `theme_oregontrail()`

Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_oregontrail()`, modeled on The Oregon Trail on an Apple II emulator: a gray window frame, a black screen, phosphor green text and marks in three shades, and an Andale Mono title.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1985)
oregon_trail <- tibble(
  party_id = 1:300,
  profession = rep(c("Banker", "Carpenter", "Farmer"), each = 100)) |>
  mutate(profession = factor(profession,
           levels = c("Banker", "Carpenter", "Farmer")),
         median_days = c(Banker = 140, Carpenter = 155,
                         Farmer = 170)[as.character(profession)],
         days_to_oregon = round(rlnorm(n(), meanlog = log(median_days),
                                       sdlog = 0.2))) |>
  select(party_id, profession, days_to_oregon)
labs_grp_boxplots <- labs(
  title = "The Oregon Trail",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Days for 100 parties of each profession to reach Oregon",
  x = "Profession", fill = "Profession",
  y = "Days to reach Oregon")
ggp2_grp_boxplots <- ggplot(data = oregon_trail,
       aes(x = profession,
           y = days_to_oregon,
        fill = profession)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 2/3,
      show.legend = FALSE)
ggp2_grp_boxplots +
  labs_grp_boxplots
```

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a categorical variable**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a numeric (continuous) variable**
:::

::::

## Description

Grouped box plots display five different statistical measures across a series of categories, or groups, of a categorical variable.

The five statistical measures are 1) the first quartile, 2) the second quartile, and 3) the third quartile. The fourth and fifth values are the largest/smallest values no further than 1.5 X inter-quartile range from the hinges.

## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::

Install packages.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_grp_boxplots
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

In *The Oregon Trail*, you picked a profession before you set out, and it decided how much money (and how many supplies) your party started with. We'll simulate how many days it took 100 parties of each profession to reach Oregon. Each profession gets its own typical trip length (`median_days`), and `rlnorm()` draws each trip from a log normal distribution, so a few unlucky parties (dysentery, broken axles, lost oxen) take much longer than the rest. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 300 trips every time you run the code below.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_grp_boxplots
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1985) # same 300 parties every time the code runs
oregon_trail <- tibble(
  party_id = 1:300, # 300 different wagon parties, one row each
  profession = rep(c("Banker", "Carpenter", "Farmer"), each = 100) # 100 parties per profession
  ) |>
  mutate(
    profession = factor(profession,
      levels = c("Banker", "Carpenter", "Farmer")), # fastest to slowest
    median_days = c(Banker = 140, Carpenter = 155, # typical days on the trail
                    Farmer = 170)[as.character(profession)], # (looked up for each profession)
    days_to_oregon = round(
      rlnorm(n(), meanlog = log(median_days), # trips cluster near the median
             sdlog = 0.2) # with a longer tail of slow trips
      )
    ) |>
  select(party_id, profession, days_to_oregon)
glimpse(oregon_trail)
```
:::

## Distribution

Grouped box plots compare five summary numbers across groups. When the data are skewed, those five numbers aren't evenly spaced: the median sits closer to the bottom of the box, and the upper whisker is longer than the lower one. With only 100 trips per profession, sampling noise can hide this, so not every box below looks this way. Below we'll move from the trips, to a picture, to the formula.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first eight trips (all bankers).

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_grp_boxplots
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(oregon_trail$days_to_oregon, 8)
```
:::

These trips took between 112 and 180 days. The summary below shows each profession's quartiles. Only for bankers is the distance from the median up to the third quartile (`upper_gap`) larger than the distance down to the first quartile (`lower_gap`). For carpenters and farmers, the distance down is about the same or larger.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_grp_boxplots
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
oregon_trail |> 
  group_by(profession) |> 
  summarise(q1 = quantile(days_to_oregon, 0.25), 
            median = median(days_to_oregon),
            q3 = quantile(days_to_oregon, 0.75)) |> 
  mutate(lower_gap = median - q1, upper_gap = q3 - median)
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

The box plots on the left use days. The bankers' box is lopsided: the median line sits low in the box, and the long trips stretch the upper whisker. The farmers' box leans the other way: the median sits high and the lower whisker is longer. The farmers also have a few outliers above the rest. The box plots on the right put the same trips on a log scale with `scale_y_log10()`. The log scale doesn't make every box symmetric: 100 simulated trips are too few to match the formula, and the bankers and farmers each still have one low outlier.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_grp_boxplots
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| layout-ncol: 2
ggplot(oregon_trail, aes(x = profession, y = days_to_oregon, 
    fill = profession)) + 
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 2/3, show.legend = FALSE) + 
  labs(title = "Days", x = NULL, y = "Days to reach Oregon")

ggplot(oregon_trail, aes(x = profession, y = days_to_oregon, 
    fill = profession)) + 
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 2/3, show.legend = FALSE) + 
  scale_y_log10() + 
  labs(title = "Log scale", x = NULL, y = "Days (log10 scale)")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

Each profession's trips come from a [log normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution), like the Microdrive photo sizes in @sec-violin-plots:

$$
\log(X_{\text{profession}}) \sim \text{Normal}(\log(m_{\text{profession}}), \; \sigma = 0.2), \quad m = (140, 155, 170)
$$

On the log scale, the quartiles sit $0.674\,\sigma$ above and below the center, which is why the formula's boxes are symmetric on the log scale. Back on the day scale, those quartiles become $m\,e^{-0.674 \times 0.2}$ and $m\,e^{0.674 \times 0.2}$: for bankers, about 122 and 160 days. That's 18 days below the median but 20 days above it, and the gap grows the further out you go, which is why the formula stretches the upper whiskers. Try a larger `sdlog` in `rlnorm()` and the boxes become even more lopsided.


## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::

  -   Create labels with `labs()`

  -   Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data`

  -   Map `profession` to the `x` axis and to `fill`

  -   Map `days_to_oregon` to the `y` axis

  -   Add `geom_boxplot()` and set the `alpha` to `2/3`

  -   Set `outlier.shape = NA` (so the outliers aren't drawn twice)

  -   Add each trip as a point with `geom_jitter()`

  -   Remove the legend with `show.legend = FALSE`

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_grp_boxplots
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
labs_grp_boxplots <- labs(
  title = "The Oregon Trail",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Days for 100 parties of each profession to reach Oregon",
  x = "Profession", fill = "Profession",
  y = "Days to reach Oregon")
ggp2_grp_boxplots <- ggplot(data = oregon_trail,
       aes(x = profession,
           y = days_to_oregon,
        fill = profession)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 2/3,
      outlier.shape = NA,
      show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.4,
      show.legend = FALSE)
ggp2_grp_boxplots +
  labs_grp_boxplots
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::


When a categorical variable is supplied, the plot will contain a box for each level or group. Each point is one trip, jittered left and right so the points don't overlap (`height = 0` keeps each trip at its true number of days).

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: create_graph_grp_boxplots
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_grp_boxplots <- labs(
  title = "The Oregon Trail",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Days for 100 parties of each profession to reach Oregon",
  x = "Profession", fill = "Profession",
  y = "Days to reach Oregon")
ggp2_grp_boxplots <- ggplot(data = oregon_trail,
       aes(x = profession,
           y = days_to_oregon,
        fill = profession)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 2/3,
      outlier.shape = NA,
      show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, alpha = 0.4,
      show.legend = FALSE)
ggp2_grp_boxplots +
  labs_grp_boxplots
```
:::

## More info

### Notches

Add notches to the box plot using the `notch = TRUE` and `notchwidth` arguments.[^notches]


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: notches_boxplots
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
ggp2_grp_box_notch <- ggplot(data = oregon_trail,
       aes(x = profession,
           y = days_to_oregon,
        fill = profession)) +
  geom_boxplot(
      notch = TRUE,
      notchwidth = 0.85,
      alpha = 2/3,
      show.legend = FALSE)
ggp2_grp_box_notch +
    labs_grp_boxplots
```
:::

### Outliers

Box plots display outliers using points, and we can change the color of these using the `outlier.colour` argument. Inside the `geom_boxplot()`, we map `profession` to `color` and set `outlier.colour` to `NULL` (so the outlier points take the mapped color):

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: outliers_boxplots
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '100%'
#| out-width: '100%'
#| layout-nrow: 1
ggp2_grp_box_outliers <- ggplot(data = oregon_trail,
       aes(x = profession,
           y = days_to_oregon,
           fill = profession)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(color = profession),
      outlier.colour = NULL,
      outlier.size = 2,
      notch = TRUE,
      notchwidth = 0.85,
      alpha = 2/3,
      show.legend = FALSE)
ggp2_grp_box_outliers +
    labs_grp_boxplots
```
:::

[^notches]: Each notch spans the median ± 1.58 × IQR / √n, a rough confidence interval for the median, and `notchwidth` sets how narrow the notch is compared to the box.
